chapter: Piano influences: Teddy Wilson, Tatum and Bud Powell
title: Bud Powell's verdict, 'he's fast all right'
summary: After a fast, scale-based solo for Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young, Powell's remark makes Malachi realize he needs to say something on the piano.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But one of the things that I remember that particular night was that I played a set with Lester Young, I think, and Coleman Hawkins had been playing. I think when Coleman was playing, Bud Powell had played with him. And after that, I played this set. But I think Coleman Hawkins and Lester were playing. But anyway, we were playing something kind of up-tempo. And as I was playing... I played this solo. I don't know. I guess I played about four or five choruses on the thing. And I heard Coleman Hawkins ask Bud Powell, 'How do you like him?' Bud Powell, after a pause, just like he was trying to figure out what to say, 'Well, he's fast all right.' And the fact was, that's all it was, because I really didn't know how to play Jazz the way these guys were playing it. At that particular time I was very fast with scales and runs and all of that, and as I said before, I was playing more or less in the Teddy Wilson-Art Tatum vein, which... Those were the principal things that were being done, you know. So I just ran all up and down the piano, you know. And that was Bud Powell's comment, when he answered Coleman Hawkins.
When he said that... Things like that really make a

lightbulb come on in your head if you're listening, you know. I didn't take it as an offense or anything. I took it as something that I should look into. And the fact was that I began to listen to other guys who were saying things, and practically talking or singing on the instruments, and here I was running up and down the piano with no kind of message in mind at all.

Nevertheless, I wanted to go back to that before I really got into this era of the Billy Eckstine thing, because as I said, it's the most important era of my life and it will probably be a rather extensive thing that I have to say about everybody in the band.
